lead: A cable ties a device to one place. A radio frees it, charging for that freedom in range, data rate and battery life. Five links cover most embedded products: Bluetooth Classic for audio and serial replacement, BLE for a coin-cell sensor talking to a phone, ZigBee for a mesh of meters and street lights, Wi-Fi for a camera needing megabits, and LoRaWAN for a water meter two kilometres from a tower. Each sits at a corner of the same trade-off. The requirement picks the technology.
prereq: You need: the link trade-offs of UART and RS-232 and the master-slave idea from SPI and I2C.

sections.h3: Four axes: range, rate, power, topology

blocks.text: Every radio link is judged on four axes. Range is how far one hop reaches. Data rate usually means the useful (application) rate; the airtime formula below uses the raw radio rate R, which is higher because of headers, preamble and coding. Power is the current the radio draws in mA, mostly while transmitting but also while listening. Topology is the network shape: one-to-one, a star around one master, or a mesh where nodes forward for each other.
t_air = N / R, duty = t_air / T × 100%
blocks.where: N is packet length in bits; R is raw bit rate in bit/s; t_air is airtime in seconds; T is period between packets in seconds; duty is transmit duty cycle in percent.

blocks.text: Energy per bit: E_b = P_tx / R, where P_tx is transmit power in watts. A 10 mW transmitter at 250 bit/s spends 40 µJ per bit; at 1 Mbit/s it spends 10 nJ. Long range costs joules per bit, so a LoRa node sends twenty bytes and sleeps ten minutes.

Bluetooth Classic is a 2.4 GHz frequency-hopping link. It uses 79 channels of 1 MHz and hops 1600 times a second, so a microwave oven or Wi-Fi access point spoils only a slice of time. One master with up to seven slaves forms a piconet. Basic rate is 1 Mbit/s; enhanced data rate reaches 2 to 3 Mbit/s. It carries audio and serial port profile, so a Bluetooth-to-UART module appears as a COM port.

BLE shares the band but not the packet. It uses 40 channels of 2 MHz. Channels 37, 38 and 39 are advertising channels placed between Wi-Fi channels 1, 6 and 11. An advertiser broadcasts a short packet on these channels and a scanner reads it without a connection. That is how a phone sees a fitness band before you pair it.

After connection, data moves through GATT, the Generic Attribute Profile. A server exposes services, each holding characteristics, each a small value with a 16-bit or 128-bit UUID. A client reads or writes a characteristic, or subscribes to notifications, so the sensor pushes a value only when it changes. Between connection events the radio sleeps, and the connection interval can be 7.5 ms to 4 s.

ZigBee sits on IEEE 802.15.4: 2.4 GHz, 16 channels, 250 kbit/s, offset QPSK with direct-sequence spreading. Three roles exist. The coordinator forms the network and holds the trust centre; routers have mains power and forward packets; end devices sleep most of the time. Routing is mesh, so if a lamp in a corridor fails, traffic finds another path. Smart meters and street lighting use this shape, because a 30 m hop will never cover a colony.

Wi-Fi, IEEE 802.11, uses 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz and 6 GHz. It gives 54 Mbit/s to a gigabit per second over 30 to 100 m using CSMA/CA: a station listens, waits a random backoff, then transmits. The cost is the receiver. A Wi-Fi station must stay ready for a beacon and can draw 100 mA or more, fine for a camera on mains and wrong for a coin cell.

Bluetooth, ZigBee and Wi-Fi all share 2.4 GHz and interfere. A Wi-Fi transmitter at 20 dBm easily drowns a BLE packet at 0 dBm. Three defences: channel planning, so ZigBee avoids the Wi-Fi channel in use; adaptive frequency hopping in Bluetooth, which drops bad channels; and time sharing, where the coordinator schedules around known traffic.

LoRa is a physical layer, not a network. It sends sub-GHz chirps, 865 to 867 MHz in India, spreading each symbol with a spreading factor SF from 7 to 12. Each step up in SF doubles the symbol time and so doubles the airtime for the same payload, and adds about 2.5 dB to the link budget; that extra margin is what buys the longer range. Range reaches 2 to 15 km in open ground, while the rate drops to a few hundred bit/s.

LoRaWAN is the layer above. A node transmits; every gateway in range forwards the packet to a network server, which removes duplicates and passes it to the application server. A device is not tied to one gateway and there is no pairing. Class A opens two short receive windows after each uplink and is the lowest power; Class B adds scheduled beacon slots for periodic downlink; Class C keeps the receiver on and runs from mains. The Indian band caps transmit power at 400 mW ERP, and LoRaWAN operators usually keep the duty cycle near 1 percent, so payloads stay small.

The choice follows from the requirement. Kilometres and a few bytes: LoRaWAN. Megabits: Wi-Fi. A mesh of mains nodes: ZigBee. A phone in the same room and a year on a coin cell: BLE. Audio or a serial cable replacement: Bluetooth Classic.

figure.caption: The flow reads the requirement, not the datasheet. A link needing over a kilometre goes to LoRaWAN; a megabit link goes to Wi-Fi; the short-range low-power branch splits on whether a mesh is needed.

spec.aria: A decision flow from start to range, data rate and mesh questions, leading to LoRaWAN, Wi-Fi, ZigBee or BLE and Bluetooth.

examples.question: A soil sensor sends 20 bytes every 10 minutes. Ignoring all protocol overhead, find the airtime and the transmit duty cycle for (a) BLE at a raw rate of 1 Mbit/s and (b) LoRa at 250 bit/s.
steps: Airtime ratio = 0.64 / 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ = 4000, so LoRa occupies the channel 4000 times longer for the same payload.
examples.answer: BLE: 160 µs airtime and 2.67 × 10⁻⁵ % duty; LoRa: 0.64 s airtime and 0.1067 % duty.
examples.check:
N = 20 * 8
T = 10 * 60
t_ble = N / 1_000_000
d_ble = t_ble / T * 100
t_lora = N / 250
d_lora = t_lora / T * 100
print(N)
print(f"{t_ble:.5f}")
print(f"{d_ble:.7f}")
print(f"{t_lora:.2f}")
print(f"{d_lora:.4f}")
print(f"{t_lora / t_ble:.0f}")
examples.output: BLE airtime = 160 µs = 1.6e-4 s; BLE duty = 2.67e-5 %; LoRa airtime = 0.64 s; LoRa duty = 0.1067 %; ratio = 4000

traps: BLE is not Bluetooth Classic: different packet, channels, no serial port profile or audio; not interchangeable at application level.
LoRa is the chirp physical layer; LoRaWAN is the network protocol. A LoRa radio without LoRaWAN has no addressing, gateways or device classes.
Wi-Fi is not a low-power sensor link. The receiver draws tens to hundreds of mA waiting for a beacon, so a coin cell lasts days, not years.
Sharing 2.4 GHz does not make radios compatible. BLE, ZigBee and Wi-Fi use different modulation, channel widths and MAC rules, and interfere.
Duty cycle slips: 0.1067 is a percentage, 0.001067 is a fraction. Write the unit every time.

quiz.q: Name the five wireless technologies of this chapter and the band each occupies.
quiz.a: Bluetooth Classic and BLE: 2.4 GHz. ZigBee: 2.4 GHz, IEEE 802.15.4. Wi-Fi: 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz. LoRaWAN: sub-GHz LoRa, 865 to 867 MHz in India.

quiz.q: Why does BLE place its three advertising channels at 37, 38 and 39?
quiz.a: They sit in gaps between Wi-Fi channels 1, 6 and 11, so discovery is less likely drowned by an access point.

quiz.q: A ZigBee node sends a 40-byte packet at 250 kbit/s. Find the airtime.
A LoRa packet has 1.2 s airtime and is sent every 2 minutes. Find the duty cycle and say whether it meets a 1 percent limit.
quiz.a: 1.2 / 120 = 0.01 = 1.0 percent. It just meets the limit; a longer packet breaks it.

quiz.q: A product must send 12 bytes every 15 minutes, within a 30 m room, to a phone, on a coin cell for three years. BLE or LoRaWAN? Give two reasons.
quiz.a: BLE. The phone has a BLE radio, so no gateway or network server is needed. BLE also has shorter airtime, so lower transmit energy per packet.

quiz.q: Why is Wi-Fi a poor choice for a battery-powered temperature sensor, even though it has the highest data rate?
quiz.a: Data rate is not the constraint; energy is. The Wi-Fi receiver stays ready for beacons and draws about 100 mA or more, emptying a coin cell in days. BLE or ZigBee sleep between short events.

quiz.q: State the difference between LoRaWAN Class A, Class B and Class C devices.
quiz.a: Class A opens two short receive windows after each uplink and is lowest power. Class B adds scheduled beacon slots for periodic downlink. Class C keeps the receiver on and needs mains power.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry is converging on Thread and Matter for home devices, which run IPv6 over IEEE 802.15.4 meshes and borrow ZigBee's radio. Wi-Fi 6 added target wake time so stations sleep on a schedule, narrowing the power gap with BLE. LoRaWAN is adding LR-FHSS for higher capacity; NB-IoT and LTE-M compete for metering. Search next for LoRaWAN regional parameters, BLE GATT profiles and 2.4 GHz coexistence.
